source: Griffiths & Tenenbaum (2006) Optimal predictions in everyday cognition
finding: People were asked to predict a total duration or extent from one observed value t (for example, a movie has grossed $10M; what is its total?). Median answers matched Bayesian posterior medians computed from real-world distributions, with no free parameters fitted to the human data.
numbers: Two groups: 208 and 142 undergraduates; each answered one item per class, with t drawn at random from 5 values per class. Classes: movie grosses, poem lengths, life spans, pharaoh reigns, marriages (group 1); movie run times, US House terms, cake baking, waiting times, marriages (group 2). Analysed responses: 174 grosses, 197 poems, 197 life spans, 191 pharaohs, 136 run times, 130 House terms, 126 cakes, 158 waiting.
quote: Judgments were indistinguishable from optimal Bayesian predictions based on the empirical prior distributions
limits: Fit judged by plot and the word 'indistinguishable'; no fit statistic in the main text. Marriage item dropped: 52% answered 'forever'. One judgment per person, so the match is on group medians.
agent_relevance: Prior-sensitive prediction by humans is a clean benchmark. A scaffold that uses an explicit prior over the quantity should beat a fixed add-a-constant rule.

source: Griffiths & Tenenbaum (2006) Optimal predictions in everyday cognition (three prior shapes)
finding: The prediction function changes shape with the true prior. Gaussian prior: guess pulled toward the mean. Power-law prior: guess is a constant multiple of t (about 1.5 times for movie grosses). Erlang prior: guess is t plus a constant. Humans showed all three shapes in the matching domains.
numbers: Gaussian: life spans, movie run times. Power-law: movie grosses, poem lengths. Erlang: House terms, pharaoh reigns. The single uninformative-prior rule p(t_total) proportional to 1/t_total (Gott 1993) was rejected as a rule for all domains.
limits: Prior forms were read off public data tables; shapes checked per domain, not in one pooled test.
agent_relevance: Different problem types need different priors. One default rule of thumb for estimates is wrong in many everyday domains.

source: Griffiths & Tenenbaum (2006) Optimal predictions in everyday cognition (pharaohs, waiting times)
finding: Where people lack direct experience, they know the shape of the prior but get its parameter wrong. Pharaoh reign predictions were too high; a follow-up elicited a subjective prior that fixed the fit. For waiting times, the judgments were used to infer which prior shape people assume (power-law, exponent 2.43 best fit).
numbers: Follow-up: 35 undergraduates stated a typical pharaoh reign; median 30 years, giving Erlang parameter 17.9 versus a true value of about 9.34. Waiting-time power-law exponent 2.43 best fit by least squares to median judgments.
limits: The subjective prior was fitted after seeing the misfit, so that part is partly post hoc (the extra value comes from separate data, which limits but does not remove the worry).
agent_relevance: Wrong prior parameters, not wrong inference, explain many estimate errors. A scaffold could ask for reference-class numbers first and check them.

source: Griffiths & Tenenbaum (2006) Optimal predictions in everyday cognition (cake baking)
finding: Even when the true prior is irregular (cake baking times), human predictions stayed close to the Bayesian curve. The match is not limited to smooth distributions.
numbers: Cake item: t from 10, 20, 35, 50, 70 min; 126 analysed responses.
limits: No numeric fit reported; visual comparison.
agent_relevance: Supports using empirical reference-class distributions rather than fitted parametric ones in estimation steps.

source: Vul, Goodman, Griffiths & Tenenbaum (2014) One and Done? Optimal decisions from very few samples
finding: Group-level Bayesian fits can hide that each person acts on one or a few samples from the posterior. Re-plotting the 2006 data shows the spread of individual answers matches the posterior (quantile-quantile near perfect), not the posterior median plus noise. The paper then shows that if thinking costs time, one sample per decision can maximise reward per unit time.
numbers: Fixed-k analysis: if a sample costs as much time as the action, zero samples is best (guess at random). When fewer than about 10 samples would double decision time, one sample is optimal. Optimal count rises slowly, reaching up to 75 samples only at the cheapest tested costs. SPRT and accumulator stopping rules gave nearly the same expected samples and reward rate as fixed k. The paper notes 100 samples often suffice for reasonable posterior inference but 2,500 or more may be needed for close approximation.
limits: Theory with assumed costs; the sample count is not measured directly from people. Probability-matching evidence is mixed.
agent_relevance: Supports our budget logic: a few cheap samples can be near optimal when each costs real time. Do not over-sample.

source: Perfors, Tenenbaum, Griffiths & Xu (2011) A tutorial introduction to Bayesian models of cognitive development
finding: Gives the standard formal core: posterior proportional to likelihood times prior; hypotheses defined by what data they allow; the size principle, under which a hypothesis consistent with n examples gets likelihood (1/|h|)^n, so smaller consistent hypotheses win exponentially fast (a 'suspicious coincidence').
numbers: Marble example: bag A (2 marbles) vs bag B (3). After one red marble, A is favoured by 1.5 times. After red, green, red, green, A has (1/2)^4 = 0.0625 against (1/3)^4, about 5 times as likely. The model assumes examples are sampled from the concept ('strong sampling').
quote: If people think the data were generated in some other way ... then their inferences change
limits: Tutorial, not a new experiment. If examples were chosen for other reasons, the inference changes.
agent_relevance: The size principle is a cheap checkable rule: among hypotheses that all fit the shown examples, prefer the narrowest. Matches guardrail G3 (fit is not proof).

source: Xu & Tenenbaum (2007) Word learning as Bayesian inference (as described in Perfors et al. 2011)
finding: Adults and 3 to 4 year old children saw 1 or 3 labelled examples of a novel word and picked other members from 45 objects. With one example, generalisation was graded from subordinate to superordinate. With three examples, generalisation sharpened to the narrowest level, as the size-principle model predicts.
numbers: 45 objects in 3 superordinate categories (animals, vegetables, vehicles); 1 vs 3 examples per word. Exact percentages and group sizes were not in the text read.
limits: Second-hand description, so per-condition numbers are not recorded. Read the original before citing figures. Replication and rival accounts are for other angles of this subfield.
agent_relevance: Narrow-first generalisation from several consistent examples is a way to pick the least over-general rule.

source: Perfors et al. (2011) tutorial: interpretation issues
finding: Lists the main objections to Bayesian models: 'optimal' may not mean best behaviour; the hypothesis space is chosen by the modeller; neural plausibility is unclear; models sit at Marr's computational level and may not describe process. Proposes rational process models (sampling approximations) as the bridge.
numbers: Qualitative; no numbers.
limits: Self-assessment by proponents.
agent_relevance: Same split we use: the schema is the process level; Bayesian ideas supply the standard to check against.

source: Griffiths (2020) Understanding human intelligence through human limitations
finding: Argues human intelligence should be understood as the best use of limited time, compute and communication. Presents Bayesian inference as the tool for inductive bias, and relates meta-learning to learning a prior (hierarchical Bayes).
numbers: Position paper; no experiments of its own.
limits: Perspective piece.
agent_relevance: Supports resource-rational design: use the Bayesian answer as the target and ask how few samples or steps get close.

source: Xie, Raghunathan, Liang & Ma (2022) An explanation of in-context learning as implicit Bayesian inference
finding: Argues that if pretraining text is a mixture of latent concepts (an HMM mixture), in-context learning works by implicitly inferring the shared latent concept from the prompt. Tested on a synthetic dataset (GINC).
numbers: GINC: accuracy rises with number of examples (0 to 64) and with example length k in {3,5,8,10}; 2,500 prompts per setting; 4-, 12-, 16-layer GPT-2 style transformers and LSTMs. Larger models do better even at equal pretraining loss (81% to 85% from 12 to 16 layers). Accuracy varies widely with example order.
limits: Synthetic data and small models. Theory needs a distinguishability condition on prompt delimiters. Real LLMs not tested for the mixture structure.
agent_relevance: Prompt examples act as evidence about a latent task. Longer, more informative examples help more than more of them. Order effects are expected.

source: Falck, Wang & Holmes (2024) Is in-context learning in LLMs Bayesian? A martingale perspective
finding: Tests a necessary condition of Bayesian learning on exchangeable data, the martingale property (predictions must not depend on the order of data). Finds violations and non-Bayesian shrinkage of uncertainty with more data, and concludes ICL is not Bayesian in this sense.
numbers: Three experiments (Bernoulli, Gaussian, synthetic natural language). Models: Llama-2-7B, Mistral-7B, GPT-3 (2.7B and 170B), GPT-3.5, GPT-4 on a subset. Bernoulli with n=50: most models inside the confidence intervals, main exception GPT-4; Gaussian: clear deviations from the reference posterior; natural-language case n=80, m=40 with GPT models: deviations.
limits: Synthetic exchangeable data. Checks a necessary, not a sufficient, condition. Chat-style reasoning prompts not tested.
agent_relevance: Do not trust an LLM's running credence as a calibrated posterior. Compute the update in code.

source: Zhu & Griffiths (2024) Eliciting the priors of large language models using iterated in-context learning
finding: Iterated learning (a Gibbs sampler: the LLM infers a hypothesis from data, new data is drawn from that hypothesis, repeat) recovers GPT-4's implicit prior. Priors elicited on causal strength, proportion estimation and everyday quantities qualitatively match human priors.
numbers: Everyday quantities: all six from Griffiths & Tenenbaum 2006 tested; modes matched humans. The pharaoh prior differed, with GPT-4 closer to the truth than people. Proportion task: 12 iterations. Speculative events: median GPT-4 year 2042 for superhuman AI, 2045 zero carbon, 2050 Mars colony (paper cites expert forecast of 2047 at 50%).
limits: Comparison to humans is visual (human data taken from published figures). Only GPT-4. The elicited prior is not independently verified.
agent_relevance: Priors in LLMs are human-like and can be read out with a loop. A scaffold can sample a prior instead of asking for a point guess.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in large language models
finding: On a five-round flight recommendation task with 624 simulated users, off-the-shelf LLMs fall far below a Bayesian Assistant that updates exactly, and often stop improving after round 1. Fine-tuning on the Bayesian Assistant's predictions works better than fine-tuning on the correct answers (oracle).
numbers: Final-round accuracy: Bayesian Assistant 81%, humans about 58% (48 simulated users), random 37%, off-the-shelf models roughly 36 to 51% (Gemma 2, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5, GPT-4.1 Mini, Gemini 1.5 Pro; read from figure text). After Bayesian teaching, models reach about 75 to 76% (Gemma, Llama) and agree with the Assistant about 80% of the time; oracle teaching gives lower and more variable results.
limits: Needs fine-tuning and open weights. The task has an exactly computable posterior, which many real tasks lack. Belief-based accuracy did not improve for Qwen.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that models do not update well on their own, and that a code-run Bayes update beats a model-run one.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) Bayesian teaching: prompting tests
finding: Prompt-only fixes did not help: chain of thought, numerical instead of verbal options, 30 instead of 5 rounds, and pretrained-only models all left accuracy near the original level. Adding the LLM's own verbalised posterior improved belief-based predictions but not direct prediction.
numbers: Appendix Fig 9: CoT ('Let's think step by step') similar to baseline; the non-interactive setting lowered belief-based accuracy.
quote: LLMs prompted with CoT perform similarly to those prompted in the way described in the main text
limits: Appendix results are in figures; small differences not tested in the text read.
agent_relevance: Telling the model to reason step by step does not give it Bayesian updating. Supports moving counting and updating into code.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 on classic judgment tasks: in the cab problem it treated the base rate as irrelevant, as people often do (probabilities about equal); it gave the intuitive but wrong answers on the CRT; it did well on bandit tasks.
numbers: Bandit regret over 13,000 problems and the horizon task: GPT-3 mean regret 2.72 (SD 5.98) vs humans 3.24 (SD 10.26), a significant difference; GPT-3 initial regret in long-horizon tasks lower than humans, t(5550) = -4.07.
limits: Early GPT-3 model; small rewording of vignettes broke good results, which the authors read as limited robustness.
agent_relevance: Base-rate neglect in an LLM is a prior failure: a scaffold needs an explicit prior step.

source: McCoy & Griffiths (2023) Modeling rapid language learning by distilling Bayesian priors into artificial neural networks
finding: Meta-learning (MAML) on languages sampled from a Bayesian prior gives a neural net that learns formal languages from few examples like the Bayesian model, and also learns English syntax from naturalistic text.
numbers: English text: perplexity 19.67 prior-trained vs 19.75 standard network (p < 1e-20) and 24.4 for a smoothed 5-gram; best earlier Transformer 19.69. 40 runs for the largest model. Better on recursion and priming tests.
limits: Gain in perplexity on natural text is tiny; the benefit shows only on targeted tests. Small models and small corpus.
agent_relevance: Background: a prior can be distilled into weights. Not a scaffold technique.

source: Wong et al. (2023) From word models to world models
finding: Proposes rational meaning construction: an LLM translates language into programs in a probabilistic language of thought, and Bayesian inference over those programs does the reasoning. Covers probabilistic, relational, visual-physical and social reasoning.
numbers: Four domains, including a Bayesian tug-of-war example; no single headline accuracy was read.
limits: Mostly demonstration; limited quantitative scoring in the text read.
agent_relevance: Model translates, code computes the posterior: the same split as our schema.

source: Ernst & Banks (2002) Humans integrate visual and haptic information in a statistically optimal fashion
finding: Cue combination: people combine vision and touch weighting each by its reliability, as the maximum-likelihood rule predicts. [from memory, not opened]
numbers: Not recorded; open the paper before citing numbers.
limits: Not opened. Later work on suboptimality (Rahnev & Denison 2018) reports many failures.
agent_relevance: Weight sources by reliability, not equally.

source: Jones & Love (2011) Bayesian fundamentalism or enlightenment?
finding: Critique: many Bayesian models set priors and likelihoods after seeing data, ignore process, and are rarely compared with alternatives. Proposes Bayesian Enlightenment, joining Bayesian models to mechanisms. [from memory, not opened]
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Not opened; BBS target article with many commentaries.
agent_relevance: Check that priors were set before seeing the outcome (G3).

source: Bowers & Davis (2012) Bayesian just-so stories in psychology and neuroscience
finding: Critique: Bayesian accounts are flexible enough to fit almost any result by choosing priors, likelihoods and utilities. [from memory, not opened]
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Not opened; replies exist.
agent_relevance: Unconstrained priors make fit meaningless, the same warning as G3.

source: Tenenbaum, Kemp, Griffiths & Goodman (2011) How to grow a mind: statistics, structure, and abstraction
finding: Hierarchical Bayesian models with structured hypothesis spaces (graphs, grammars, logic programs) and learned overhypotheses as the core of probabilistic cognitive science. [from memory, not opened]
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Source for learning the prior at a higher level and for program-like hypothesis spaces.

source: Kemp & Tenenbaum (2008) The discovery of structural form
finding: A model chooses among forms (tree, ring, chain, grid, cluster) by Bayesian model selection to explain a data set. [from memory, not opened]
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Form selection by fit and simplicity could mirror choosing a representation for a problem.

source: Chater, Tenenbaum & Yuille (2006) Probabilistic models of cognition: conceptual foundations
finding: Editorial for a TICS special issue: probability as a common language for perception, learning, reasoning and language. [from memory, not opened]
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Perfors et al. (2011) tutorial: hierarchical learning of constraints
finding: Hierarchical models learn second-order knowledge (overhypotheses), for example that regions tend to be long thin rectangles, so one example informs the next. This is how a learner can have strong constraints that are themselves learned.
numbers: Toy illustrations (rectangle regions, marble bags); no human numbers in this section.
limits: Toy examples, not experiments.
agent_relevance: Experience from earlier problems can set priors for the next one.

source: Griffiths (2020) human limitations: collective sampling
finding: Shows that agents each holding one sampled hypothesis and passing beliefs to the next generation converge to the Bayesian posterior (iterated learning view). 'Yesterday's posterior is today's prior.'
numbers: Formal argument; no human data.
limits: Assumes agents sample from the right conditional.
agent_relevance: Many cheap diverse hypotheses with selection can approximate Bayes. Our samples from one model are correlated (G4), so the analogy needs care.

source: Zhu & Griffiths (2024) priors: method detail
finding: The method copies the human iterated-learning design: the LLM sees data d and returns a hypothesis h; the next data d' is drawn from p(d|h). The chain's stationary distribution equals the learner's prior if the learner samples from its posterior.
numbers: Lifespan example: new age sampled uniformly from 1 to the predicted lifespan; tmax=150 years for male lifespan, 100 years for pharaoh reigns, 120 min for cakes.
limits: Needs the model to sample, not give a modal answer.
agent_relevance: The same loop can elicit the model's own prior on a task for audit.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) generalisation
finding: Bayesian-taught models carried the skill to unseen tasks (hotels, web shopping) and to real human users, with gains over untuned models; accuracy with humans is capped because human choices are noisy.
numbers: Fine-tuned on flights only, tested on hotels and web shopping; Assistant accuracy near 80% on simulated users, lower with humans.
limits: Numbers read from figure text only.
agent_relevance: The skill is a procedure learned from examples of exact inference: teach by good traces, not by instruction.
